lead: Photo retouching keeps every edit separate from the original pixels. The photo sits on the bottom layer. Retouch strokes go above it, colour changes go in adjustment layers, and masks decide where effects appear. Filters blur, sharpen or add noise by changing small neighbourhoods. Because the correction is stored as a recipe, you can reopen it next week. Studios and news desks use this workflow to clean images safely.
prereq: You need: Chapter 5.6 for pixel tools, and the RGB colour model from Unit 1.

blocks.text: An image opens as a stack of layers. The bottom layer holds the original photo. Each layer stores a colour C and an alpha α at every pixel; α runs from 0 (transparent) to 1 (opaque). The software draws bottom first, so a layer covers the result below by its opacity.

blocks.where: C_top and C_below are upper and lower channel values; α is effective alpha after layer opacity and mask; round gives an integer and clamp keeps 0–255.

blocks.text: A mask stores grey m: white (m = 1) shows, black (m = 0) hides, grey blends. Effective alpha is α_eff = α_layer × m. You retouch through the mask; painting black hides the retouch at that spot; paint white over a blemish to show the correction.

Blend modes replace normal mixing: Normal C = C_top; Multiply C = C_top·C_below/255 (darkens); Screen C = 255 − (255−C_top)(255−C_below)/255 (lightens); Overlay C = 2·C_top·C_below/255 when C_below < 128, else 255 − 2(255−C_top)(255−C_below)/255 (adds contrast).

An adjustment layer stores a correction, not a result. Levels, curves and hue/saturation are common. The adjustment affects every layer below it unless you clip it. Clipping makes it affect only the layer directly beneath, which is the local fix.

Filters are neighbourhood operations. Blur replaces a pixel by a weighted average of nearby pixels. Sharpen increases local contrast. Noise adds random variation. Unsharp mask forms original minus a blurred copy, then adds a scaled version of that difference back to the original to strengthen edges. Keep filters on a separate layer so the amount can be changed later.

Order matters. Put the retouch layer above the background, then a curves adjustment above it to correct both. If the curves must not touch the retouch, move the curves adjustment below the retouch layer (directly above the background) or clip it to the background layer. Only a few universities teach this chapter, so focus on the model, not menus.

figure.caption: The stack has a curves adjustment on top, a masked retouch layer in the middle and the original photo at the bottom. The mask limits the retouch while the curves correction can affect every layer below it.

spec.aria: A layer stack with a curves adjustment on top, a masked retouch layer in the middle and the original background at the bottom.

examples.question: A background pixel is (200, 100, 50). A blue fill layer (0, 0, 255) lies on top with layer opacity 50% and a mask value of 40% white at that pixel. Find the composite pixel.
steps: All values lie in 0–255, so the rounded result is (160, 80, 91).
examples.check:
bg=(200,100,50)
top=(0,0,255)
a=0.5*0.4
out=[]
for b,t in zip(bg,top):
    v=round(a*t+(1-a)*b)
    out.append(max(0,min(255,v)))
for v in out:
    print(v)

traps: An unclipped adjustment layer changes every layer below it, not just the layer you were looking at.
Effective alpha is layer opacity times mask value; forgetting the mask makes a faint retouch look full strength.
The composite must be rounded and clamped to 0–255; normal alpha compositing averages values already in 0–255, so clipping comes from additive blends or adjustments, not from normal stacking.
Multiply darkens and screen lightens; swapping them reverses the correction.
Sharpening cannot recover detail that was never captured; it only raises local edge contrast.

quiz.q: What does a black mask value do at a pixel?
quiz.a: Hides the layer there; m = 0 gives α_eff = 0.

quiz.q: Why is an adjustment layer called non-destructive?
quiz.a: It stores the correction, not changed pixels; original layers remain editable.

quiz.q: A layer has opacity 50% and a mask value of 50% white. Find α_eff.
Background (100,100,100), top (200,0,0), opacity 50%, mask 100%. Find the composite pixel.
Why do clipped highlights appear when an additive blend or an adjustment pushes a channel above 255?
quiz.a: Normal alpha compositing averages values already in 0–255 and stays in range; additive blends or strong adjustments can exceed 255, and clamping cuts at 255 and removes colour differences.

quiz.q: What does multiply blend do to channel values?
quiz.a: Multiplies and divides by 255; result is ≤ each input, so the image darkens.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern editors add content-aware fill, frequency separation for skin and neural filters. Smart objects and adjustment layers use the same recipe idea. Search for frequency separation, luminosity masks and non-destructive workflow. AI inpainting is the research edge, but it still writes into a layer.
